RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria:
Haematuria is blood in the urine. Three questions frame it. (1) Is it really blood? — a positive dipstick needs red cells confirmed on microscopy; a positive dip with no red cells is myoglobin or haemoglobin, and red urine can be beetroot, rifampicin or menstrual contamination. (2) Visible or non-visible, painful or painless? (3) What is the source? — urological (tumour, stone, infection: clots, timing within the stream, colic) versus glomerular (dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts, proteinuria, hypertension, AKI). The rule that carries the topic: painless visible haematuria in an adult is a urological cancer until proven otherwise (see bladder cancer, renal cell carcinoma), while a nephritic picture is a glomerulonephritis that can cost the kidneys in days (see glomerulonephritis).
🚨Two haematurias are emergencies. Painless visible haematuria — especially aged ≥45, a smoker or with aromatic-amine / dye exposure — is bladder / renal / upper-tract cancer until excluded → 2-week-wait referral for flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram (see bladder cancer). A nephritic picture — haematuria with proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine (± red-cell casts, dysmorphic red cells) — is a glomerulonephritis / rapidly progressive GN / vasculitis that can destroy nephrons within days → urgent nephrology and immunology (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, see vasculitis, AKI). Also act on clot retention (catheter / irrigation) and an infected obstructed system (fever + loin pain + obstruction → emergency decompression).

1Triage & screen
🔍Is it really blood?
  • Confirm red cells on microscopy — a positive dipstick alone is not enough
  • Positive dip, no red cells → myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) or haemoglobinuria (haemolysis)
  • Exclude beetroot, rifampicin, doxorubicin and menstrual contamination
🚩Painless visible haematuria = cancer
  • Bladder cancer (commonest), renal cell carcinoma, upper-tract TCC, prostate — painless and visible is the alarm
  • Risk: age ≥45, smoking, aromatic amines / dyes, prior pelvic radiotherapy, cyclophosphamide
  • 2-week-wait → flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram (see bladder cancer, RCC)
🚩The nephritic emergency
  • Dysmorphic red cells / red-cell casts + proteinuria + hypertension + AKI = a glomerulonephritis
  • Rapidly progressive GN / vasculitis can lose the kidneys in days → urgent nephrology (see glomerulonephritis)
  • Send ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, ANA and consider a renal biopsy (see vasculitis)
🟣Urological, non-malignant
  • Stones: colicky loin-to-groin pain + haematuria (see renal stone disease, loin-to-groin pain)
  • Infection: cystitis / UTI (dysuria, frequency) or pyelonephritis (fever, loin pain) (see UTI, pyelonephritis)
  • BPH, trauma / catheter, schistosomiasis (travel, terminal haematuria) (see BPH)
🟢Localise & characterise
  • Timing in the stream: initial = urethral · terminal = bladder base / prostate · total = bladder / upper tract
  • Clots mean a urological (not glomerular) source; worm-like clots suggest the upper tract
  • Colic → stone · painless → cancer · LUTS → prostate (see LUTS)
🩺Investigate
  • Urine: dipstick + microscopy (red-cell morphology, casts) + MSU culture; ACR / PCR for proteinuria
  • Bloods: U&E / eGFR, FBC, clotting, and BP
  • Imaging: CT urogram (or ultrasound) + flexible cystoscopy; nephrology bloods + biopsy if glomerular
Confirm the blood, then find the source. Prove red cells on microscopy, then split urological (clots, colic, painless visible = cancer) from glomerular (dysmorphic cells, casts, proteinuria, hypertension, AKI). Painless visible haematuria = 2-week-wait; a nephritic picture = urgent nephrology.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain:
Loin pain is pain in the flank / renal angle. The first split is renal / urological vs referred. Renal pain has renal-angle tenderness, urinary features (haematuria, dysuria, see haematuria) and often fever; referred pain comes from the musculoskeletal spine (movement-related), herpes zoster (dermatomal), the chest (basal pneumonia / pleurisy) or the gut. The next split is character: colicky loin-to-groin pain in a patient who cannot lie still is ureteric colic from a stone — its own topic (see loin-to-groin pain) — whereas constant, dull loin pain suggests infection, obstruction, a mass or a referred cause. Two emergencies hide here: an infected obstructed kidney and a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (see AAA).
🚨Two loin pains can kill. Fever + loin pain + an obstructing stone is an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) — pus under pressure → emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) plus antibiotics, before rapid sepsis (see pyelonephritis, stone). A leaking / ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm presents as sudden flank / back pain + collapse or hypotension + a pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath — do not mistake it for renal colic → CT angiogram or straight to theatre (see AAA, pulsatile mass). And obstruction of a single / solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction causes AKI / anuria and needs urgent decompression (see AKI).

🔍Renal or referred?
  • Renal: renal-angle tenderness, haematuria / dysuria, fever — think kidney / ureter
  • Musculoskeletal: movement-related, paraspinal tenderness, no urinary features (see back pain)
  • Other referred: herpes zoster (dermatomal ± rash), basal pneumonia / pleurisy (see pneumonia), biliary / bowel
🚩Infected obstructed kidney
  • Fever + loin pain + obstruction (stone) = pyonephrosis — pus under pressure
  • A urological emergency → decompress (nephrostomy / stent) + antibiotics + resuscitate
  • Can become septic quickly; a solitary or bilateral obstruction also causes AKI / anuria (see pyelonephritis)
🚩The AAA mimic
  • Sudden flank / back pain + collapse / hypotension + pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath
  • Leaking / ruptured AAA — classically mistaken for renal colic, especially a first “stone” over 60
  • → CT angiogram or straight to theatre; do not delay (see AAA, pulsatile mass)
🟣Renal / urological causes
  • Pyelonephritis and renal / perinephric abscess; obstruction / hydronephrosis (stone, clot, PUJ, tumour)
  • Renal cell carcinoma (mass, haematuria, weight loss, see RCC); polycystic kidneys (bleed / infection, see inherited kidney disease)
  • Renal infarction / vein thrombosis (AF, nephrotic, thrombophilia, see renal vascular); papillary necrosis
🟢Character & pattern
  • Colicky loin-to-groin, cannot lie still → ureteric stone — its own topic (see loin-to-groin pain)
  • Constant, dull → infection, a mass, obstruction or a referred cause
  • Bilateral loin pain → bilateral obstruction, polycystic kidneys, or medical renal disease
🩺Investigate
  • Urine dipstick + MSU culture; bloods: U&E / eGFR, FBC / CRP, blood cultures if febrile
  • Imaging: CT KUB (stone / obstruction), ultrasound (hydronephrosis), contrast CT for abscess / infarction
  • CT angiogram if an AAA is possible — before labelling a first “stone” in an older patient
Renal or referred, colicky or constant. Renal-angle tenderness + urinary features + fever = a kidney problem; colicky loin-to-groin = a stone (its own topic). Never miss the infected obstructed kidney (fever + obstruction → decompress) or the leaking AAA hiding as a first “renal colic” over 60.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin Pain:
Loin-to-groin pain is the classic presentation of ureteric colic — a stone passing down the ureter. It is sudden, severe and colicky (waves), and the patient is characteristically restless and writhing (unlike peritonitis, where they lie still). The pain radiates from the loin to the groin, and on to the scrotum / labia as the stone descends; a stone at the vesicoureteric junction adds bladder irritability (frequency, urgency). Most have haematuria (see haematuria) and vomiting. Confirm with a non-contrast CT KUB. This is a broad topic’s stone half (see loin pain): recognise the colic, but always exclude the mimics — a leaking AAA in the older patient (see AAA) and an ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age — and act on the infected obstructed stone and AKI.
🚨“Renal colic” is a diagnosis of exclusion in the wrong patient. A first episode over 60, or colic with hypotension or a pulsatile mass, is a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm until the aorta is imaged → CT angiogram, not a CT KUB (see AAA, pulsatile mass). In a woman of reproductive age, do a pregnancy test — an ectopic pregnancy presents as groin / iliac-fossa pain. Fever + an obstructing stone is an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) → emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) + antibiotics (see pyelonephritis); and obstruction of a solitary or both kidneys causes AKI / anuria (see AKI).

1Recognise & exclude
🔍Recognise the colic
  • Sudden, severe, unilateral loin-to-groin pain in waves; the patient is restless / writhing (not still)
  • Radiation tracks the stone: loin → groin → scrotum / labia; a VUJ stone adds frequency / urgency
  • Usually haematuria and vomiting (see haematuria)
🚩Exclude the AAA
  • First colic over 60, hypotension or a pulsatile mass → a leaking AAA, not a stone
  • Image the aorta (CT angiogram) before accepting “renal colic” in an older arteriopath
  • A ruptured AAA is rapidly fatal if mislabelled (see AAA)
🚩Infected obstruction & AKI
  • Fever + an obstructing stone = pyonephrosis → emergency decompression + antibiotics (see pyelonephritis)
  • Obstruction of a solitary or both kidneys → AKI / anuria (see AKI)
  • These override the “wait for the stone to pass” approach
🟣Other mimics
  • Ectopic pregnancy: reproductive-age woman with iliac-fossa / groin pain → pregnancy test
  • Testicular torsion: acute scrotal pain, high-riding testis — examine the scrotum (see testicular torsion, acute scrotal pain)
  • Appendicitis / diverticulitis / biliary depending on side and site
🟢Stone facts that steer it
  • Size: <5 mm usually pass spontaneously; >10 mm rarely do
  • Site: the VUJ is the commonest place to lodge; also PUJ and the pelvic brim
  • Type: calcium oxalate (commonest), uric acid (radiolucent on X-ray, seen on CT), struvite (staghorn, infection), cystine
🩺Investigate
  • Urine dip (blood in ~90%, but absence does not exclude) + MSU; pregnancy test in women
  • Bloods: U&E / eGFR, calcium, urate, FBC / CRP
  • Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard; ultrasound in pregnancy / young patients
Restless with loin-to-groin colic and haematuria = a stone — confirm with non-contrast CT KUB. But first exclude the AAA (older, pulsatile, hypotensive) and the ectopic (pregnancy test), and act on the infected obstructed stone (fever → decompress).

Restless writhing is the tell. A patient who cannot lie still has colic (a stone), whereas someone who lies motionless has peritonism. Confirm the stone on CT KUB — but never let a classic story stop you excluding the AAA and the ectopic.

At the bedside — confirm the colic, exclude the mimics, relieve the pain
History & red flags
Sudden colicky loin-to-groin pain, restlessness, radiation, haematuria, vomiting, LUTS, fever, prior stones, dehydration / diet / gout, pregnancy risk, AAA risk
Examine
Cannot lie still (vs peritonism), renal-angle tenderness, abdomen for a pulsatile mass, the scrotum, observations for sepsis; pregnancy test and urinalysis
Investigate
Non-contrast CT KUB; urine + MSU; U&E, calcium, urate, FBC / CRP; ultrasound if pregnant / young; CT angiogram instead if an AAA is possible
Act
Analgesia (NSAID first-line, e.g. PR diclofenac; opioid if needed) + antiemetic + fluids; small distal stones → expectant + medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blocker); large / failed / obstructing → ureteroscopy / ESWL / PCNL; infected obstruction or AKI → emergency decompression

Small stones pass with analgesia ± an alpha-blocker; larger ones need intervention — then a metabolic work-up (calcium, urate) and prevention (hydration, diet, ± thiazide / allopurinol / citrate).

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria:
Dysuria is pain or burning on passing urine. Two questions sort it. (1) Internal or external? — internal dysuria (felt inside, throughout voiding) points to the bladder or urethra; external dysuria (stinging as urine passes over inflamed vulval skin) points to a vulvovaginal cause. (2) Where is the source? — bladder (cystitis / UTI: frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine), urethra (urethritis / STI: discharge, sexual history, see discharge), vagina (candida / other vaginitis), prostate (a man with fever and perineal pain) or the upper tract (pyelonephritis: fever + loin pain). The commonest cause is bacterial cystitis in a woman — but always consider an STI in the young / sexually active, and distinguish uncomplicated (a healthy non-pregnant woman) from complicated (men, pregnancy, children, catheter, recurrent, structural).
🚨Some dysuria is more than cystitis. Fever + loin pain + rigors is pyelonephritis / urosepsis → treat and consider admission (see pyelonephritis). A man with fever, perineal pain and a tender prostate has acute bacterial prostatitis — risk of retention; avoid vigorous prostatic massage and give a prolonged antibiotic course. Do not miss an STI — dysuria + urethral discharge is urethritis; screen, treat and arrange partner notification (see urethritis). Dysuria + visible haematuria in an older smoker needs a bladder-cancer work-up (see bladder cancer, haematuria). In pregnancy, treat even asymptomatic bacteriuria (with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic); in men and children, investigate the underlying cause.

1Triage & screen
🔍Internal or external?
  • Internal (felt inside, throughout voiding) → bladder / urethra (cystitis, urethritis)
  • External (stinging as urine passes over the vulva) → vulvovaginal cause (candida, atrophy)
  • The split separates a UTI / STI from a vaginitis
🟣Bacterial cystitis / UTI
  • Commonest, especially in women: frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy / offensive urine
  • Dipstick: nitrites + leucocytes (± blood); usual organism E. coli
  • Uncomplicated (healthy non-pregnant woman) → treat empirically (see UTI)
🚩Upper tract & prostate
  • Pyelonephritis: fever + loin pain + rigors → treat, consider admission (see pyelonephritis)
  • Acute prostatitis (a man): fever, perineal pain, a tender boggy prostate, LUTS — retention risk
  • Avoid vigorous prostatic massage; prostatitis needs a prolonged antibiotic course
🟣Urethritis / STI
  • Younger / sexually active, often with urethral discharge (see discharge)
  • Chlamydia (commonest), gonorrhoea, Mycoplasma genitalium (see chlamydia, gonorrhoea)
  • Screen with NAAT, treat, and arrange partner notification (see urethritis)
🟢Vaginitis & other
  • Candida (itch, curdy white discharge, see candidiasis), trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis
  • Atrophic vaginitis (postmenopausal, external dysuria and dryness)
  • Also stones, catheter, chemical irritant and interstitial cystitis (bladder pain, sterile urine)
🩺Investigate & who to culture
  • Dipstick (nitrites / leucocytes / blood); a dip may suffice in a healthy woman
  • MSU culture in men, pregnancy, children, complicated / recurrent cases and treatment failure
  • STI NAAT if urethritis; vaginal swab if vaginitis; do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria except in pregnancy
Internal vs external, then the source. Most dysuria is bacterial cystitis in a woman — treat empirically. But screen for an STI in the young, treat pyelonephritis and prostatitis as more than cystitis, and investigate men, children, pregnancy and recurrence.

At the bedside — localise the source, decide who to culture

Internal vs external, frequency / urgency / suprapubic pain, discharge, sexual history, fever / loin pain, pregnancy, catheter, recurrence, haematuria

Temperature and observations, suprapubic / loin tenderness, external genitalia (discharge, ulcers, atrophy), a gentle DRE if prostatitis is suspected; dipstick the urine

The rules that carry it: split internal vs external and localise the source. Treat uncomplicated cystitis empirically; culture men, pregnancy, children and failures. Escalate for pyelonephritis and prostatitis, screen and treat STIs, treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy, and work up haematuria for cancer.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary Tract:
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are the cluster of bladder-emptying and bladder-storage complaints. The organising split is storage (irritative) — frequency, urgency, nocturia, urgency incontinence — versus voiding (obstructive) — hesitancy, a weak / intermittent stream, straining, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying — plus post-micturition dribble. That split targets the cause and the treatment: voiding LUTS in an older man is usually benign prostatic hyperplasia (see BPH), while storage LUTS suggests an overactive bladder or bladder irritation (UTI, stone, cancer). A DRE and urinalysis anchor the assessment (see prostate on DRE). Throughout, screen for the red flags: visible haematuria (cancer, see haematuria), retention (see acute / chronic) and a neurological cause.
🚨LUTS can hide serious disease. Visible haematuria with LUTS is bladder or prostate cancer until excluded (see bladder cancer); persistent irritative symptoms in a smoker can be carcinoma in situ. Chronic retention (a painless, palpable bladder with a high residual, overflow incontinence and a rising creatinine) is obstructive uropathy → catheterise / decompress (see chronic retention); acute retention is painful and needs immediate catheterisation (see acute retention). Cauda equina presents with LUTS plus saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms and faecal incontinence → emergency MRI (see cauda equina). A hard, nodular prostate, bone pain or a raised PSA points to prostate cancer (see prostate cancer).

🔍Storage vs voiding
  • Storage (irritative): frequency, urgency, nocturia, urgency incontinence
  • Voiding (obstructive): hesitancy, weak / intermittent stream, straining, terminal dribble, incomplete emptying
  • The split targets the cause and the drug (overactive bladder vs outlet obstruction)
🟣The prostate (men)
  • BPH: a smooth, enlarged prostate with voiding LUTS — commonest cause in older men (see BPH)
  • Prostate cancer: a hard, nodular prostate, bone pain, raised PSA (see prostate cancer)
  • Always examine the prostate (see prostate on DRE)
🚩Cancer & haematuria
  • Visible haematuria + LUTS → bladder / prostate cancer until excluded (see bladder cancer)
  • Persistent irritative LUTS in a smoker can be carcinoma in situ
  • → flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram (see haematuria)
🚩Retention & neurology
  • Acute retention: painful, palpable bladder → catheterise (see acute retention)
  • Chronic retention: painless, high residual, overflow, rising creatinine → decompress (see chronic retention)
  • Cauda equina: LUTS + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral legs + faecal incontinence → emergency MRI (see lower back & spine)
🟢Bladder & systemic causes
  • Overactive bladder (storage), UTI (see UTI), bladder stone, interstitial cystitis
  • Neurogenic bladder: MS, spinal-cord disease, Parkinson’s, diabetes
  • Polyuria (diabetes / diabetes insipidus, see polyuria), diuretics, caffeine, constipation

  • Post-void residual (bladder scan), flow rate / urodynamics, ultrasound; cystoscopy if haematuria
Storage vs voiding drives the plan. Voiding LUTS in an older man is usually BPH; storage LUTS is an overactive bladder or irritation. A DRE and urinalysis are mandatory — and screen every case for haematuria, retention and a neurological cause.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary Retent:
Acute urinary retention is the sudden, painful inability to pass urine, with a palpable, tender, distended bladder. It contrasts with chronic retention, which is painless and high-volume (see chronic retention). The commonest cause is benign prostatic hyperplasia in an older man (see BPH), usually with a precipitant — constipation, a new drug (anticholinergic, opioid, decongestant), a UTI, alcohol or recent surgery. The immediate job is to relieve it: catheterise and record the residual volume drained, then find and treat the cause (see urinary retention). Always screen for the emergencies: cauda equina and high-pressure retention with AKI.
🚨Relieve first, then think. Insert a urethral catheter immediately (a suprapubic catheter if urethral fails) and record the residual volume (typically 500–1000 mL; relief of pain confirms it). Cauda equina presents as retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, back pain and faecal incontinence → emergency MRI and surgery — do not simply catheterise and discharge (see lower back & spine). High-pressure retention (bilateral hydronephrosis, a raised creatinine) risks post-obstructive diuresis after decompression — monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids (see AKI). Clot retention (heavy haematuria) needs a 3-way catheter and irrigation, not a standard catheter (see haematuria).

1Relieve & screen
🔍Recognise it
  • Sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a palpable, tender suprapubic bladder (dull to percussion)
  • Confirm with a bladder scan; typically 500–1000 mL is drained
  • Contrast with chronic retention — painless, large-volume (see chronic retention)
🚩Catheterise & measure
  • Insert a urethral catheter to relieve it; a suprapubic catheter if urethral access fails
  • Record the residual volume drained; relief of the pain confirms the diagnosis
  • Clot retention → 3-way catheter + irrigation (see haematuria)
🚩Cauda equina & neurology
  • Retention + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg symptoms + back pain + faecal incontinence = cauda equina
  • → emergency MRI and surgery; do not just catheterise and discharge (see lower back & spine)
  • Also consider spinal cord compression, MS and diabetic autonomic neuropathy
🟣Find the cause (men)
  • BPH (commonest, see BPH); prostate cancer (hard nodular prostate, see prostate cancer, prostate on DRE)
  • Urethral stricture, clot retention (see bladder cancer), phimosis / paraphimosis
  • UTI / prostatitis can precipitate it (see UTI)
🟢Precipitants
  • Constipation, drugs (anticholinergics, opioids, sympathomimetics / decongestants), alcohol
  • Post-operative / post-anaesthetic (especially spinal / epidural), immobility, UTI
  • Women (less common): pelvic mass / prolapse, post-partum, Fowler’s syndrome
🩺Investigate & watch
  • Urinalysis + MSU, U&E (renal function), FBC; DRE and abdominal exam
  • After decompression, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis (urine output + U&E, replace fluids)
  • Renal ultrasound if AKI / high residual; PSA is unreliable acutely — defer it
Catheterise now, record the residual, then find the cause. Acute retention is a painful, palpable bladder — relieve it immediately. The commonest cause is BPH + a precipitant, but always screen for cauda equina and watch for post-obstructive diuresis after a high-pressure decompression.

Painful = acute, painless = chronic. Acute retention hurts and is usually BPH plus a precipitant — treat the trigger (constipation, a drug, a UTI). But a rising creatinine with hydronephrosis means high-pressure retention, and saddle / bowel symptoms mean cauda equina.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — relieve, then find the cause and the red flags
History & red flags
Onset and pain, time of last void, prior LUTS (see LUTS), haematuria, new drugs, constipation, back / neurological / bowel symptoms, recent surgery / anaesthetic
Examine
Palpable, tender, dull suprapubic bladder; DRE (prostate, faecal impaction, anal tone); a focused neurological exam (saddle, legs); genitalia (phimosis); dipstick the urine
Investigate
Catheterise + record residual; MSU, U&E, FBC; renal ultrasound if AKI / high residual; MRI if cauda equina; defer PSA (unreliable in acute retention)
Act
Catheterise immediately; treat the precipitant (relieve constipation, stop the drug, treat UTI); start an alpha-blocker and plan a trial without catheter; monitor for post-obstructive diuresis; refer urology; cauda equina → emergency MRI + surgery
Then — confirm the cause
BPH-related retention → residual + DRE (± delayed PSA)Prostate cancer → PSA + MRI + biopsyCauda equina → emergency MRIClot retention → 3-way catheter + cystoscopyHigh-pressure retention → U&E + renal USS
The rules that carry it: a painful, palpable bladder = acute retention — catheterise and record the residual. Treat the precipitant, start an alpha-blocker before a trial without catheter, and always screen for cauda equina and high-pressure retention (post-obstructive diuresis).
